title: Uniforms outdoors, Lincoln Park and race and color in New Orleans
summary: Uniforms were for street work and Lincoln Park picnics; talk turns to the mixed audience, light-skinned Creoles, his white wife and his Indian mother, and a doctor's record party.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Did you wear that uniform when you played in the club?

Well, we didn't wear the uniform in the club. We wore the uniforms that we played. In the streets. In the streets. We didn't, but, see, when we played in the club, after we come out of the club, we had so much, you see, we had so much work that we wore uniforms. Like, we would most of the players at big picnics like Lincoln Park. See, the Colors had a place they called Lincoln Park. We had a ball of Lincoln Park. But a balloon used to go up every Sunday evening. We played all out there, you know. That place would be loaded.
Was the audience at Lincoln Park mainly Negro? Yeah. Or were they white people too? Was it mixed or was it almost all?

No. Well, it worked. You see, sometimes the world would come in there and say, because they got the Negroes on in all of these. You know, if they were the colors of them. Uh-huh. Just like my wife. You see, my wife is white. She's white. Uh-huh. But as my wife looked, a lot of people that, but no one from New Orleans, my wife from New Orleans would say, no, well, she looked just like those Creoles down there. The Creoles in New Orleans are very fair. Yeah. Blonde, red-haired, and everything else. See, they got everything. Yes. In our race.
You take my mother. My mother was a full-blooded Indian. Uh-huh. Because my mother is very polite. She's the same tribe as Pee-Wee Russell.
No, from, uh. Uh, my mother's not from Oklahoma. She's from the hills of Virginia. Oh, yeah.
Up in them hills. Is that so? Yeah.
And, uh, they're very fair. Because you, we're, we're, I had a lot of friends, white boys who come out there, Italian boys.
Out to Lincoln Park? Yeah. Did you play at the, at Lincoln Park, March, yourself?

Never played at the, like. See, you got bad blood in mama. Yeah. You need a needle, sticky, it's really bad. So that old preacher living, or doctor living in the house, so he, I played for him, he said, I'm having a little part tonight, first can I borrow that record. And a bunch of preachers he had, this doctor, a friend of mine, started lending him this record, and all the doctors, and all the women sitting in there. And you know, I didn't want to hear that record.
And, uh, and that's, and they liked them kind of things. What you think they wouldn't like, that's what they like. Sure. Always.
